name: A Black Hole in a Universe Filled by a Scalar Field
description: Schwarzschild's black hole in a massless scalar field whose gradient far away points along one axis, the scalar counterpart of Ernst's black hole in Melvin's magnetic universe. Somasri Sen and Narayan Banerjee wrote the metric down in 2001, and Vitor Cardoso and José Natário found it again in 2024. The field is smooth on the horizon, and the curvature grows without bound far from the axis.
convention: The mass parameter $m = GM/c^2$ is a length and the gradient $b$ an inverse length. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.

coordinates.name: Spherical

parameters.description: Mass parameter, a length, $m = GM/c^2$ with $M$ the mass of the black hole

Gradient of the scalar field far out along the axis, an inverse length; the field is $\varphi = \sqrt{c^4/4\pi G}\,b\left(r - m\right)\cos\theta$, with $R_{\mu\nu} = (8\pi G/c^4)\,\partial_\mu\varphi\,\partial_\nu\varphi$, and $b = 0$ is Schwarzschild's metric
The factor that shrinks distances along $r$ and $\theta$, equal to 1 on the axis and on the horizon

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ of Somasri Sen and Narayan Banerjee and of Vitor Cardoso and José Natário, Schwarzschild's at $b = 0$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ a length. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Scalar Universe

parameters.description: Gradient of the scalar field, an inverse length; the field is $\varphi = \sqrt{c^4/4\pi G}\,bz$, with $R_{\mu\nu} = (8\pi G/c^4)\,\partial_\mu\varphi\,\partial_\nu\varphi$, and $b = 0$ is flat space

coordinates.convention: We use cylindrical coordinates $(t, \rho, \phi, z)$ about the axis the field points along, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\rho$ and $z$ lengths, for the universe with no black hole, $m = 0$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
